figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: One physical world versus diverse virtual worlds. Left: Agents learn from varied physical scenes sharing common dynamics, where they can scale and generalize with broader experience (Wang et al., 2026a). Right: Agents play diverse games with varying dynamics. We want to investigate the question that whether continued pre-training scales and generalizes in virtual worlds.
figures.headline: Physical scenes share one set of dynamics, whereas game worlds differ in dynamics, so the study tests transfer across virtual worlds.
citing_sentences: In Figure 1, virtual worlds remove much of this consistency.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Adaptation to the keyboard–mouse interface during CPT. Smoothed training losses for key, mouse, and format tokens, and eight-direction mouse prediction accuracy for three model capacities trained on mixtures S1 and S4.
figures.headline: Key, mouse and format training losses fall during continued pre-training, while eight-direction mouse accuracy keeps improving across model sizes.
citing_sentences: Figure 2 illustrates the action component losses.
Figure 2 shows the training loss of key, mouse, and format tokens.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Loss scaling across data volume, model size and data diversity. Rows report the smoothed training loss and three-level validation loss. Columns 1–4 denote the 0.8B-27B backbones; colors denote the training mixtures S1–S5; markers denote the six checkpoints from 50 to 1,600 hours. The base model loss is annotated in each validation panel. All plots in a given row shares a common y-axis scale. Column 5 plots the loss predicted by the fitted scaling law (Section 4.4) against the observed loss.
figures.headline: Validation loss drops with data on Minecraft and in-corpus sets, while out-of-distribution loss stops improving after early training.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 presents the three-level training and validation losses alongside our scaling law predictions.
After exposure to 50 hours of training data, validation losses drop below those of the base models on all three validation sets (Figure 3), even for games absent from the training mixture.

From 50 to 1,600 hours, the mean Minecraft validation loss decreases by about 10.4% across four model sizes under the MineCraft-heavy mixtures S1–S3, correlating with substantial gains in MCU performance (Figure 3).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Benchmark performance across data budget, model size and data diversity. Rows report MCU, ViZDoom, OmniGameArena, and GameWorld performance. Columns denote the six checkpoints from 50 to 1,600 hours. Colors denote S1-S5 and the base-model reference, while each curve spans the 0.8B-27B backbones. All plots in a given row shares a common y-axis scale.
figures.headline: Benchmark scores rise with data on in-corpus worlds, while GameWorld scores fall for the largest model as data grows.
citing_sentences: Coupled with the marginal CPT gains on GameWorld in Figure 4, this suggests that CPT improves learning within the corpus but does not keep improving on distant worlds.

Figure 8 replots the 100 scores of Figure 4 with gameplay hours on the horizontal axis and one column per model size, so the duration dynamics of Section 4.1 can be read directly: the monotone gains of 0.8B and 2B under every mixture, the flattening of 9B and 27B after 100–400 h, the decline of S1 at 9B and 27B on OGA and ViZDoom, and the decline of every 27B mixture on GameWorld.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: A training window with sparse reasoning. Five consecutive 200 ms turns from an Apex Legends recording in S4. Each turn begins with the current frame. Only $o_{t}$ and $o_{t+4}$ carry a GPT-5.6-Luna rationale; the other three turns emit an empty <think> span and act directly. Every action packet contains a mouse displacement $(\Delta x,\Delta y)$ and the keys held during six 33 ms sub-steps; key icons show the distinct keys in each packet. Image tokens receive no loss, while thought and action tokens are trained autoregressively. Rationales are abridged excerpts of the stored annotations.
figures.headline: Five consecutive turns show sparse reasoning, with rationales on two turns and empty think spans on the other three.
citing_sentences: Figure 5 shows five consecutive turns from an S4 training window, two with rationales and three without.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Frontier progress on the four benchmarks against release date. Circles: GPT series; squares: Qwen series; stars: GameScaling S3 models at 1,600 h, all under time-paused interaction.
figures.headline: Successive GPT and Qwen releases score higher on the four benchmarks under time-paused play, and GameScaling S3 is placed alongside them.
citing_sentences: Frontier models have advanced on gaming benchmarks (Figure 6), and our GameScaling models prove highly competitive with both Minecraft specialists and frontier models in 3D environments (Section 5).
Figure 6 shows substantial improvements in gameplay across successive GPT and Qwen models under time-paused evaluation.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Loss scaling against model size. Rows: training loss at the checkpoint, and held-out validation loss on Minecraft, on the game-balanced in-corpus set, and on the out-of-distribution set; columns: 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, and 1,600 gameplay hours; colors: mixtures S1–S5.
figures.headline: At each duration, validation losses on three sets are plotted against model size for all five mixtures.
citing_sentences: Figure 7 replots the losses of Figure 3 with model size on the horizontal axis and one column per duration.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Benchmark scaling against gameplay hours under time-paused interaction. Rows: MCU, ViZDoom, OGA, and GameWorld (all in %); columns: 0.8B, 2B, 9B, and 27B backbones; points span 50 to 1,600 gameplay hours; colors: mixtures S1–S5; dashed gray: the untrained Qwen3.5 backbone.
figures.headline: Scores for 0.8B and 2B rise steadily with gameplay hours, while 9B and 27B flatten after 100–400 h.
citing_sentences: Figure 8 replots the 100 scores of Figure 4 with gameplay hours on the horizontal axis and one column per model size, so the duration dynamics of Section 4.1 can be read directly: the monotone gains of 0.8B and 2B under every mixture, the flattening of 9B and 27B after 100–400 h, the decline of S1 at 9B and 27B on OGA and ViZDoom, and the decline of every 27B mixture on GameWorld.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Test-time scaling on MCU. Cumulative success rate of GameScaling-0.8B-S1 and GameScaling-9B-S1 (1,600 h, solid) and their untrained Qwen3.5 backbones (dashed) on the 30 MCU tasks as a function of the maximum steps allowed, on a logarithmic axis. The standard protocol uses 600 steps.
figures.headline: Cumulative MCU success against allowed steps shows how much remaining failure reflects the 600-step budget.
citing_sentences: Figure 9 asks how much of the remaining failure is a step budget rather than a competence limit.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Three-factor laws with prediction bands. Rows are the training loss, the Minecraft validation loss and the in-corpus validation loss; columns are the mixtures S1–S5; colors are model sizes. The horizontal axis is gameplay hours, from 100 h for the training loss and from 50 h for the validation losses. Points are measurements, lines are the single fitted law of each row evaluated at that panel’s $(N,r)$, and shaded bands are the 5–95% range of the law over $B=300$ stratified case-bootstrap replicates. The last column is predicted against observed loss; per-panel RMSE is printed.
figures.headline: The three-factor law fits training, Minecraft and in-corpus losses across mixtures S1 to S5, with bands from bootstrap replicates.
citing_sentences: Evaluated on the original grid, the replicate laws change the RMSE by at most $0.0004$ for the Minecraft law and $0.0001$ for the in-corpus law, and the 5–95% bands in Figure 10 are narrower than the markers over most of the grid.

abstract: Scaling data, diversity and model capacity has improved embodied learning in physical environments, where diverse experiences remain grounded in shared physical laws. Whether these gains extend to virtual worlds with different visual styles, dynamics, controls, and objectives remains unclear. We investigate this question through a controlled study of continued pre-training (CPT) across three axes: data volume, diversity, and model size. Our 120 training configurations span four model sizes from 0.8B to 27B, six data budgets from 50 to 1,600 hours, and five mixtures ranging from Minecraft-only data to diverse multi-world corpora. We assess performance and generalization using three-level validation losses and gameplay benchmarks from in-corpus worlds to unseen worlds. Our results show: (1) more data improves in-corpus performance, diversity improves transfer to related worlds with limited gains in distant worlds, and model size improves data efficiency but generalizes worse to distant worlds under single-world training; (2) we observe an early interface phase with broad cross-world benefits and a later world phase with gains narrowed to in-corpus and related worlds, and fit an empirical scaling law relating validation loss to data volume, diversity and model size; and (3) our models are competitive with Minecraft specialists and frontier models in 3D worlds, and perform best in real-time settings. However, the limits of imitation and persistent gaps in distant worlds suggest that building generalist embodied agents requires richer training stages beyond continued pre-training.

sections.body: The paper asks whether continued pre-training on gameplay trajectories generalizes across virtual worlds that differ in visuals, dynamics, controls and objectives, or whether heterogeneous data interferes with learning in each world. The authors run a controlled grid of 120 configurations spanning 0.8B to 27B models, 50 to 1,600 hours of data and five mixtures from Minecraft-only to multi-game corpora. Evaluation uses three-level validation loss and gameplay benchmarks: in-corpus worlds such as Minecraft and Doom, unseen related worlds in OmniGameArena, and unseen distant worlds in GameWorld. The introduction also reports a scaling law fit with R² values of 0.982 and 0.995 on Minecraft and in-corpus loss.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Virtual worlds vary in visuals, physics, controls and goals, so the study asks whether heterogeneous gameplay data helps or interferes.

sections.body: The section groups related work into three areas: environment-specific deep reinforcement learning agents for Atari, Go, StarCraft II and Dota 2; recent game foundation models such as VPT and NitroGen, which use continued pre-training as a common mechanism; and scaling studies in language, GUI and robotics. It also covers games as test environments, citing Minecraft and Doom suites, OmniGameArena and GameWorld. The authors state that no prior work systematically isolates data volume, diversity and model size while measuring held-out loss and transfer at varying distances from training.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Earlier virtual-agent work used single-environment specialists or foundation models, and none isolated data, diversity and model size together.

sections.body: Each step takes a prompt, the current observation and interaction history, produces a reasoning trace, and then a keyboard-mouse action chunk covering 200 ms. The model receives observations at 5 Hz and controls at 30 Hz, with 20 turns per trajectory. The grid crosses four Qwen3.5 backbones (0.8B, 2B, 9B, 27B), six budgets from 50 to 1,600 hours, and five mixtures S1 to S5. Gameplay makes up 85% of training data and general vision-language data 15%. Minecraft share across S1 to S5 is 100%, 51.4%, 27.1%, 2.8% and 0%. The grid totals 3.5×10^11 training tokens and 2.2×10^22 FLOPs. Evaluation uses validation losses plus three gameplay levels: in-corpus MCU and ViZDoom, related OmniGameArena, and distant GameWorld.
sections.heading: Preliminaries and Experiment Framework
sections.headline: The study frames gameplay as reason-then-act steps and trains a 120-configuration grid over model size, data budget and mixture.

sections.body: Scaling is tested along data volume, mixture diversity and model size across all 120 configurations. Data scaling shows an interface phase in which losses fall even for games absent from training, followed by a world phase in which mean Minecraft validation loss decreases by about 10.4% from 50 to 1,600 hours under S1 to S3, while out-of-distribution loss stagnates or rises. For OmniGameArena, the mean score across S2 to S5 is roughly 2.8 times S1 at 1,600 hours. Larger models match given performance with up to a 32× less gameplay data, but for 27B under S1 GameWorld falls by roughly 17 points. A three-factor law fits training and in-corpus losses (R² 0.980 and 0.995) but not out-of-distribution loss, which gives beta approximately 0.
sections.heading: Scaling and Generalization in Heterogeneous Virtual Worlds
sections.headline: More data and diversity improve in-corpus and related-world results, but gains in distant worlds stay limited.

sections.body: Table 1 reports MCU success on 30 tasks against Minecraft specialists and general game models. The 27B-S1 model outperforms the best specialized model by 13 points, and 0.8B-S3 completes 36% of tasks, while behavior-cloning models trained on tens of thousands of hours score near zero on instruction-conditioned tasks. Table 2 compares four benchmarks under time-paused and real-time settings. Under real-time interaction, GameScaling-9B-S3 scores higher than the best tested frontier model. In GameWorld, frontier models score twice as high as the authors' models. In real-time play every frontier model suffers an approximate 90% score reduction on ViZDoom and MCU, while the 0.8B to 9B models retain 88% of their time-paused performance.
sections.heading: Comparing with Frontier Models
sections.headline: Models are competitive with Minecraft specialists and frontier models in 3D worlds and lead frontier models in real-time play.

sections.body: The discussion argues that scaling must pair with corpus curation: under a limited budget the training mixture should mirror the target environment, and a strong in-domain loss fit does not guarantee reliable play in distant worlds. Real-time play depends on response latency as well as capability, so the authors ask future comparisons to report response times and deployment infrastructure. Compared with its base model, the 27B-S3 checkpoint improves the time-paused OmniGameArena score by 16.0 points but drops 4.0 points on GameWorld. The authors attribute the gap possibly to imitation without environmental feedback, insufficient game coverage, or both.
sections.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
sections.headline: Gains in related worlds do not reliably reach distant worlds, and the imitation objective may help explain the gap.

sections.body: The gameplay training data come from the publicly released VPT, D2E and OpenP2P datasets under their respective licenses. The authors state that these datasets were cleaned by their providers to protect player privacy. They sample existing gameplay trajectories and add retrospective reasoning annotations, without collecting new gameplay recordings or personal data. The section states that no additional ethical concerns arise from these procedures.
sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.headline: Training uses publicly released gameplay datasets under their licenses, and the authors collect no new recordings or personal data.

sections.body: The appendix gives dataset and mixture accounting, including the effective number of worlds D for each mixture: 1.0 for S1, 14.5 for S2, 35.2 for S3, 60.1 for S4 and 58.7 for S5. It describes the out-of-distribution validation set, built from 28 games and 4,480 clips, with exactly 160 clips per game across 92 sessions. Reasoning annotations are sparse: 5.4% to 6.0% of assistant turns include reasoning, and rationales average 64.5 to 65.4 tokens. Training used about 45,000 H200 GPU-hours for one seed per condition. Further sections compare the grid with D-CPT, CMR and When Data Is Scarce scaling studies, and list GUI and robotics studies in tables.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers mixture accounting, the out-of-distribution validation set, sparse reasoning annotations and comparisons with related scaling studies.
